metaDescription: Click-through rate is clicks divided by impressions. What a normal organic CTR looks like by position, and why AI Overviews have pushed the old curve down.
definition: Click-through rate is the share of impressions that turn into clicks — clicks divided by impressions, expressed as a percentage.
answer: Click-through rate is clicks divided by impressions. In Search Console it tells you how often people who saw your result chose it. The CTR curve everyone quotes — around 31% for position one — comes from a 2019 study of a pre-AI-Overview web. On queries with an AI Overview, expect materially less.
takeaways: CTR = clicks ÷ impressions. Simple arithmetic, routinely misread because of how it aggregates.
The famous ~31.7% for position one is **Backlinko's 2019 analysis**. It describes a SERP that no longer exists.
AI Overviews measurably reduce clicking. Pew and Ahrefs both found it in 2025; they disagree on how much.
Branded queries inflate your sitewide CTR. Always split branded from non-branded before drawing a conclusion.

body: A link to your site appearing in results someone sees is an [impression](/glossary/impressions). Them clicking it is a click. CTR is one divided by the other.

The complication is aggregation. Sitewide CTR averages across every query, page, country and device, so it moves without anything changing. Pick up impressions on a broad query you rank 40th for and it falls, even though every page performs exactly as before.
So the number is only useful filtered: one query, one page, India versus everywhere else, mobile versus desktop. Unfiltered CTR is a mood indicator, not a metric.

callout.title: The comparison that actually works
callout.body: Filter to a single query, then compare its CTR against what that position typically returns. Below par at position 3 means your title and snippet are losing a contest you'd already won — one of the few SEO problems you can fix in an afternoon.

sections.h2: The curve everyone quotes is from 2019
body: Ask anyone what CTR position one gets and you'll hear about 31%. That comes from Backlinko's 2019 analysis of five million Google searches. Good study — of a SERP with no AI Overview, a smaller ad block and fewer features. That page has changed shape considerably since.
Published curves are useful as priors. They are not measurements of your SERP. Here's how we use them when forecasting, stated as assumptions rather than facts.

bullets: **The ranges are wide on purpose.** Anyone quoting CTR to one decimal place for your query is quoting someone else's dataset, and query type moves this more than position does.

sections.h2: What AI Overviews did to it
body: Two 2025 analyses are worth knowing together, because they measured different things and got different answers.

Pew Research Center studied real browsing behaviour and found users clicked through to a result on roughly half as many visits when an AI-generated summary was present. Ahrefs, studying a large keyword set, reported top-ranking pages seeing around a third lower CTR on queries carrying an AI Overview.
Neither is India-specific and neither is your site. They agree on direction and rough magnitude: the drop is real, big enough to matter to a forecast, and hardest on informational queries.

The practical version is arithmetic. Take the 2019 figure of roughly 31%, take a third off, and you land near 20% — which is why we forecast nearer 20% than 30% wherever an AI Overview appears. A derived assumption, not a measured 2026 statistic, and we'd rather label it than dress it up.

callout.title: Falling CTR with flat position isn't a failure
callout.body: It's the signature of a SERP that grew a feature. Before anyone rewrites the page, check whether an AI Overview or a local pack appeared above it. Rewriting a page to fix a layout change wastes a month and fixes nothing.

sections.h2: Branded versus non-branded, and why the split matters
body: Someone searching your company name has already decided; they're using Google as a navigation bar. Branded CTR runs many times higher than non-branded, so a healthy sitewide number is often brand demand in disguise.
Split it: filter queries containing your brand name, note that CTR, then invert the filter with "Queries not containing". The second number reflects how well your pages compete against strangers.

It also explains the pattern that panics founders in month four: sitewide CTR drops while everything improves. New non-branded impressions arrive at low positions and dilute the branded average. The business is growing; the blended metric is falling. Both are true.

sections.h2: Improving CTR, and when not to bother
body: CTR is one of the few SEO fixes with a same-week payoff: you're editing what appears in the result rather than moving the result. Work the queries where you rank 3–10 and underperform.
numbered: **Rewrite the [title tag](/glossary/title-tag) around the promise, not the keyword.** Google rewrites titles it finds unhelpful, so a stuffed one often isn't what's shown.
**Write the meta description as ad copy.** It isn't a ranking factor; it's the only sentence you fully control in the result.
**Add a number, price or date** where it's genuinely true. Specificity separates your result from four near-identical ones.
**Ship schema that changes the result's appearance** — FAQ, breadcrumb, review where legitimately applicable.
**Match the query's language.** If people search in Hinglish and your title is formal English, the result reads as something else.
bullets: **When not to bother:** position 11+, or low CTR on queries you shouldn't rank for. Nothing you write changes a result nobody scrolls to, and irrelevant impressions cost you nothing real.

faqs.q: What is a good CTR in SEO?
faqs.a: There's no universal figure — it depends almost entirely on position, query type and which features sit above you. The useful benchmark is your own: compare a query's CTR to what your other queries return at the same position. Consistently below that, the title and snippet are the problem.

faqs.q: Is CTR a Google ranking factor?
faqs.a: Google has repeatedly said it doesn't use CTR directly as a ranking signal, while acknowledging that user interaction data feeds into its systems. The practical answer is to stop arguing about it: a better click-through rate brings more visitors regardless, which is the point.

faqs.q: Why did my CTR drop while my rankings stayed the same?
faqs.a: Almost always a SERP layout change — an AI Overview, an expanded ad block or a local pack appearing above you. Your position didn't move; the page grew. Check the live SERP before assuming the page needs rewriting.

faqs.q: How do I see CTR for a single keyword?
faqs.a: In Search Console's Performance report, add a query filter for the exact term, then read the CTR for that filtered view. Compare it against the same query in a previous period rather than against a published curve, which was measured on somebody else's SERPs.

faqs.q: Does a high CTR with no conversions mean anything?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's usually an intent mismatch. You've written a result compelling enough to click and a page that doesn't do what the click promised. That combination burns budget quietly, because the traffic chart looks healthy while the pipeline doesn't move.
